summary: Specifies how to use the DES encryption algorithm in output feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines DES output feedback mode for Telnet's encryption option. It describes the initial vector, key identifier, and limits of the method.

questions: how does des ofb work with telnet
how does telnet des ofb64 start
subtitle: Command and key-handling rules for DES output feedback in Telnet encryption.

tldr.problem: This RFC specifies how the Telnet encryption option uses DES in 64-bit output feedback mode.
tldr.mechanism: The peers exchange an 8-byte initial vector, confirm it, negotiate a key identifier, and process data with DES_OFB64.
tldr.outcome: The RFC notes that output feedback does not provide data integrity and says cipher feedback offers limited detectability of modification.

today: RFC 2953 is an Informational memo specifying a Telnet encryption option. The unit metadata lists no later update or replacement.

sections.title: The Initial Vector Commands
sections.content:
The encryption type is DES_OFB64. The side that has WILL ENCRYPT generates an 8-byte random initial vector and sends it in an OFB64_IV command in clear text.

The side with DO ENCRYPT replies with OFB64_IV_OK or OFB64_IV_BAD. The memo says an OK reply is required for backward compatibility; BAD is relevant when the vector violates the protocol, such as by having the wrong length.
sections.plainLanguage: One side sends an 8-byte starting value before encrypted data begins. The peer confirms or rejects that value.

sections.title: Key Negotiation and Data Processing
sections.content:
After OFB64_IV_OK, the encrypting side negotiates a key identifier using ENC_KEYID. Once a common key identifier is found, the peers may use START and END commands to control encrypted data.

The RFC explains how to reinitialize encryption state when a new vector or key identifier arrives. It also describes use of default keys associated with Telnet authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: After agreeing on a starting value, the peers select a shared key identifier. The RFC specifies how a change to either value resets the encryption state.

sections.title: Integrity Limitations
sections.content:
Output Feedback encryption does not ensure data integrity. The RFC says an active attacker may be able to substitute text if the attacker can predict the clear text.

The memo recommends Cipher Feedback instead because it provides limited detectability of data modification, while noting that neither mode provides true integrity. Adding a message authentication code would increase the bytes sent per character.
sections.plainLanguage: Output feedback can hide data but may not reveal that someone changed it. Cipher feedback can make some changes detectable, but the RFC says it still does not provide true integrity.
